model:step|title:i cut an llm s screen w.content_excerpt: Read-only Windows MCP server: delta canvas, pixel grid + UI Automation tree to cut agent vision tokens. A read-only, observation-only MCP server for Windows that bundles four screen-observation capabilities into one package — it never clicks or types anything. doctor checks dependencies, takes a trial screenshot, and spins up the server as a smoke test (verified on the development machine: 28 tools). Fovea and pixel-grid need a license key — everything else works right away. Their core is closed-source and license-gated (see License ); without a key, fovea_start / live_start fail with a clear error, but screenshot and the UI tree still work. or drop the file at the default path %USERPROFILE%\.super-computer-agent\license.lickey . Fovea is the default; a full-screen screenshot is the last resort, for when things are genuinely hard to read any other way. Priority order: fovea_step -> fovea_look (precise reading) -> ui_fuse (element names/positions, as text) -> wait_stable (wait) -> a new keyframe ( fovea_start ) -> only then screenshot . Details and the exact conditions for using screenshot : docs/WORKFLOW.md . The server enforces this ordering through tiering tags on tool descriptions, NEXT: hints after results, warnings on repeated probing, and a guard-rail on screenshot (it requires a valid reason , checked against the current session; set SCA_SCREENSHOT=free to disable it). See the last section of docs/WORKFLOW.md . Fovea ( fovea_start -> fovea_step ): instead of sending a full screenshot every time (expensive — models are billed by pixel count), it sends only what changed. Fovea is not a rewrite from scratch — it is an upgrade layer wrapped directly around the older grid-compression core ( canvas_v6 / v7 / delta2 / delta3 ), adding a 64-frame scene memory ( RECALL #k ), precise 1:1 zoomed reads ( fovea_look ), an HWND lock plus a lightweight UIA signature check to catch focus-switch races, and a hard cap on the cell store. The frame-diffing algorithm itself is closed-source, shipped only as a compiled .pyd . Pixel grid ( live_start / grid_now / ui_fuse /...): a different trade-off — instead of a real image, the screen becomes a grid of colored characters (one character per tile, encoding hue + brightness), which is far cheaper for a model to read as a general layout overview than a picture. This module's core is closed-source in full (not just the hot path), also shipped only as a compiled .pyd . Both cores are gated by the offline Ed25519 license check

model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast hig.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. story|title:a background agent to fix br.content_excerpt: Use the GitHub Action arnaudrenaud/fix-with-agent to automatically fix your code whenever a dependency update breaks your test suite: Do you rely on a test suite that gives you enough confidence to blindly merge pull requests from automatic dependency update bots such as Dependabot or Renovate? If so, you’re already saving time compared to manual updates and regression testing. Yet, you may still be sitting on a backlog of unmerged pull requests because of breaking changes following major updates (and even, sometimes, minor ones…). Now that AI helps attackers exploit vulnerabilities faster, you’d better have AI help you patch them as soon as possible and keep up with major version upgrades over the years. Of course, pulling the faulty branch and asking your local agent to “fix tests following dependency update” should do the trick with little supervision. Still, the operation induces friction: Let’s automate everything but the last two steps: reviewing and merging will remain up to you. There is no need to orchestrate our agent manually when its boundaries can be defined as follows: Here is an example of workflow for a Node.js, NPM-managed project: it fixes failing tests in Renovate pull requests using action arnaudrenaud/fix-with-agent . With this workflow, if your test suite fails following a Renovate pull request and the agent manages to fix it, you’ll see the following changes in the pull request: a comment has been published, reporting obstacles encountered and decisions taken (the same report is mentioned in the commit body and action output): Here is only one example of a small, circumscribed task that can be completed with an autonomous background agent. Let’s take the time to spot the recurring, well-defined tasks that can be performed on the side either on a fixed schedule or following a specific event. This way, we’ll clear not only the core of the task, but also the mental load of getting notified and making time for it.

Teams at AUMOVIO developed different ways to access LLMs, including provider integrations and gateways built for specific use cases. Together, these approaches highlighted the value of a shared operating model for managing our AI workloads with a single AI gateway solution AUMOVIO's cross-functional AI taskforce brought together stakeholders from security, data protection, business areas and IT. The taskforce decided on one central AI Gateway as the shared route for LLM access and governance , establishing a common direction for model access across the company. Building an AI gateway is straightforward, but operating one as an enterprise service is a permanent commitment: provider APIs change, dependencies need patching, security requirements evolve, and users need support. story|title:introducing unity gateway in.content_excerpt: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models. But agent traces can reveal other opportunities to save. At Databricks, trace analysis surfaced several: offline replays showed no performance gain from upgrading from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, so we stayed on the cheaper 4.8; fixing common MCP errors recovered an estimated $1.2M in costs a year ; and traces showed that simple prompts were going to expensive models, prompting us to adopt Smart Routing . Today, we’re introducing Unity Gateway Insights , which automatically uses Genie to analyze millions of agent traces alongside your business data and ontology. It surfaces where tokens are being wasted: MCP errors that keep recurring, simple tasks running on expensive frontier models, and repeated workflows worth turning into shared skills, all in the context of your business and under the same governance as your other data. If you already have traffic flowing through Unity Gateway, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report for the last day, 7 days, or 30 days. Insights then writes a report on the tokenomics of your coding agent rollout that answers the following questions: You can add up to 10 questions of your own to a report, such as whether the newest model is worth it for your team's work. Finding this kind of waste requires a full record of every step of every agent session: inputs and outputs, tool calls, subagents, intermediate steps, latency, and token cost. Insights runs the investigation we developed while rolling out coding agents to thousands of Databricks engineers. It samples sessions and groups them into workstreams by kind of work. story|title:microsoft agent framework co.content_excerpt: Two releases of agent-framework , Microsoft’s official Python metapackage for its Agent Framework, steal credentials from any environment that installs them. Nothing has to import the package. A .pth file runs the stealer each time Python starts, so a pip install in a CI job is enough. It takes environment variables and credential files. It also asks Azure DevOps, Azure managed identity and, in the second release, GitHub Actions for fresh tokens, and sends those out too. SafeDep flagged version 1.26.1 22 minutes after it reached PyPI on 17 November 2026. By then the attacker was close to publishing again. Once 1.26.1 came off PyPI, 1.26.2 shipped the same stealer under different file names, and SafeDep flagged it 4 minutes after upload. Removing one version did not stop an attacker who could still publish. The last clean release is 1.26.0. Update (18 November 2026): PyPI shows that vibiret , an account created on the day of the attack, can publish to agent-framework and five related projects. Four of those projects install with agent-framework. See A maintainer account created the same day . PyPI lists two maintainers for the project, microsoft and vibiret . The project gets about 192,000 downloads a month. How many installs the two bad versions got is not known yet. Static analysis of the wheel finds the .pth hook, the collector and the webhook.site endpoint. PyPI no longer serves 1.26.1. The payload moves to new files and adds GitHub Actions OIDC theft. Every release from 1.20.0 through 1.26.0 shipped a wheel and an sdist. Both malicious versions are a single wheel. The 1.26.1 wheel is 10,402 bytes, up from 6,681 in 1.26.0. A metapackage that always shipped both files now ships one. Missing provenance does not set the bad wheels apart. PyPI has no attestation for 1.26.0 either, so a consumer had no cryptographic way to tell Microsoft’s uploads from the attacker’s. story|title:microsoft s agent framework.content_excerpt: Compromised agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on PyPI use .pth startup hooks to exfiltrate Azure, GitHub Actions, and CI/CD credentials. The Microsoft agent-framework PyPI package was compromised on November 17th, affecting versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint. Avoid installing either version; if installed, remove them and rotate potentially exposed credentials. On Python startup, the .pth file imports a module that launches collection in a background process/thread. Version 1.26.1 routes through agent_framework_meta.pth → agent_framework_meta/**init**.py → agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py ; 1.26.2 uses af_runtime_diag.pth → af_runtime_diag.py . The code gathers credential-related environment variables, local config/credential files, and other processes’ environments. It also requests cloud/workflow identity tokens (including Azure in both versions and GitHub Actions OIDC in 1.26.2). It serializes the results, compresses and Base64-encodes them, then POSTs them to the same concealed webhook.site endpoint: https[://]webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb agent_framework_meta.pth executes on interpreter startup through Python’s site processing: agent_framework_meta/__init__.py adds a supposedly diagnostic hook that imports and starts the payload, suppressing errors: agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py collects credentials asynchronously. Its startup guard is inherited by child processes; on Unix, it forks and detaches. Platforms without fork use a daemon thread. Fresh process trees can trigger collection again; there is no persistent on-disk execution marker. af_runtime_diag.pth replaces the original startup hook with a single line that imports the new top-level payload: af_runtime_diag.py starts collection on import. The legitimate package initializer is restored byte-for-byte, so inspecting only agent_framework_meta/__init__.py misses this version. The collector adds GitHub Actions OIDC token requests: They inspect environment variables, other processes’ environments, credential files, and cloud identity endpoints. They actively request fresh Azure managed-identity and CI federation tokens rather than merely copying existing secrets. Collected JSON is zlib-compressed, base64-encoded, and POSTed to the decoded webhook with ?t=telemetry . Encoding provides no confidentiality

story|title:murmur efficient long contex.content_excerpt: TL;DR: Murmur speeds up long-context ASR models on audio up to 1 hour by 2.5× on average (up to 2.9×), end to end including diarization. It also lowers speaker-attributed error (tcpWER) compared with WhisperX by 7-17 points on English meetings and 10-51 points on Mandarin. Single pass, Murmur, and WhisperX transcribing the same 32-minute AMI meeting on one H100, replayed at 8×. Recent long-context ASR models, such as Microsoft VibeVoice-ASR and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize, process an hour or more of audio in a single pass. They generate text, timestamps and speaker labels at the same time. An hour of audio is tens of thousands of audio tokens (about 27,000 for VibeVoice-ASR), so a single pass is slow: on one H100, VibeVoice-ASR takes about 2.5 minutes to transcribe a 44-minute meeting. These models can also fall into a repetition loop, which makes the whole request fail. The other common approach is to split the recording into short chunks, such as the 30 s chunks WhisperX uses for Whisper. Timestamps and speaker labels then have to be stitched together across hundreds of chunk boundaries, which lowers accuracy, especially in speaker attribution. This design was built for short-context models, while long-context models can take in minutes of audio at once. Neither option fits long-context models well. We revisit how long audio should be chunked and served for these models, and design Murmur, an inference system that closes the gap between the two approaches. We first study how chunk size affects long-context ASR. Across 4 datasets and 2 languages (English and Mandarin), error drops quickly as chunks grow from 30 s and levels off within a few minutes (Figure 1). At 330 s, chunked decoding already improves on or matches single pass on word error rate (WER) and time-constrained word error rate (tcpWER) in most cases, so the model does not need the whole recording in one pass. Figure 1. Error vs. chunk size (30-390 s) for MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize and VibeVoice-ASR on four meeting datasets. Dashed lines are single pass. Error drops quickly from 30 s and levels off by about 150-330 s, mostly on the speaker metrics (cpWER, tcpWER). Figure 2. (a) WhisperX decodes 30 s segments independently and adds timestamps and speakers afterwards. (b) Long-context models decode the whole recording in one pass. story|title:parallel agent requests can.content_excerpt: Two coding-agent sessions sharing one Ollama slot waited a median 46 seconds for a response to start, against one second with a slot each. Over half the prompt tokens the server processed were repeats. Why hybrid models lose their place, and which settings change it. Ask a coding agent to fix a failing test. It might read a file, run the test, edit a function, then run the test again. Each time a tool returns a result, the agent sends another request to the model. From your terminal it looks like one conversation. From the server’s side it’s a series of increasingly long prompts, most of which it has already seen. Normally, that repetition is cheap. The server keeps the work it did on the previous turn and picks up where the new text begins. Now open a second terminal and give the same agent a task in another project. Both sessions send the same tool descriptions and much of the same setup text, but each has its own instructions and history. What happens to the first session’s work while the server answers the second? We tried this at Tensward with two unmodified Qwen Code sessions running against Ollama. When both sessions took turns on one slot (the place where the server holds an active request’s model state), the median request waited about 46 seconds for the response to start. When we gave each session a slot of its own, it waited about one second . Two sessions sharing a slot have to wait for each other. We expected some queueing. What surprised us in the logs was how much work the server did while they waited. With a shared slot, 54% of the prompt tokens it processed were repeats . With a slot each, that fell to 0.4%. Imagine pausing the server just after it reads token 8,921 of session A. Up to this point, sessions A and B are identical. The model is in exactly the state B needs. But the server keeps reading A, and B arrives only after A’s prompt is finished. Can the server get back to that moment? In a model that uses full causal attention throughout, the server keeps a pair of vectors for each token in each attention layer: a key and a value . Together these entries form the KV cache . Reading token 8,922 adds another entry. The entries for tokens 1 through 8,921 stay as they were, because earlier tokens cannot attend to later ones. As long as those entries are still in memory, the server can keep that prefix, discard A’s suffix, and start processing B where the prompts diverge. Qwen3.8-27B is a hybrid. story|title:quadgate 4 gate control plan.content_excerpt: 4-Gate discriminative control plane for AI agents: preserves KV caches, cuts LLM cost 76.9%, and achieves 3.95x median speedup. 4-Gate discriminative control plane that preserves KV caches, cuts LLM cost 76.9%, and achieves 3.95x median speedup. QuadGate is an open-source 4-gate discriminative control plane for AI coding and knowledge agents that preserves KV prefix caches, enforces offline security invariants, routes subagents by Expected Cost of Completion, and audits completion to achieve 76.9% lower cost, 3.95x median speedup (71.1% lower mean latency), and 100.0% pass@1. It runs as a persistent localhost daemon ( 127.0.0.1:8787 ), cold-session reverse proxy ( 127.0.0.1:8788 ), and zero-dependency < 450 ms hook shim ( qg-shim ) across Antigravity (including native Swarms), Claude Code , OpenAI Codex CLI , and MCP clients without spending output tokens on generative critics. Full signed receipts, SHA-256 task hashes, and methodology are published in benchmarks/reports/v1_release_proof.md (mirrored in benchmarks/reports/LATEST_PROOF.md ; 210 total receipts across 105 matched Baseline vs. QuadGate pairs over 3 runs using live gemini-decision-1 on cloud-eligible coding tasks and local Air-Gap routing elsewhere), backed by ECE calibration profiles in benchmarks/reports/calibration_decision1.json and benchmarks/reports/calibration_onnx_local.json . All totals include Gate 4 1-Strike retry tax and live classifier compute cost. Resilience Model: qg-shim enforces a < 450 ms socket deadline ( SHIM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 0.450 ). Gates 1, 3, and 4 fail-open if the daemon is unreachable; Stage-2A security rules in Gate 2 always fail-closed . QuadGate decouples gate algebra from classifier backends via ClassifierDriver ( quadgate/drivers/base.py ) and conformal probability calibration ( Temperature Scaling / Isotonic Regression , enforcing ECE <= 0.05 ). CalibrationEngine.candidate_budget_for_driver allocates up to 800 candidates per pass for parallel cloud drivers ( decision1 , jev ) and narrows local CPU cross-encoders ( onnx_local , layaa ) to 32 candidates via Pass-0 SQLite FTS5 pre-filtering. An attacker hijacking the account could use it as a distribution channel in supply-chain attacks, potentially leading to data theft or code execution. However, the researchers demonstrated a stealthier attack: they modified the model's weights so it produced audio that differed from the input text, without changing the underlying application code. Because only the weights change, there is no malicious code or signature for malware scanners to detect, the researchers say. "We changed what this model says by fine-tuning its neural weights. Same input text. Same voice file. Same configuration. Same inference code — not a single line touched in the application that runs it," said security researcher Alon Hertz . Kokoro is an open-weight model that converts text into speech. It supports multiple languages and has more than 50 voice presets. Although its developer, Hexgrad, has not pushed an update since April 2025, the project continues to be popular, with nearly 13 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face. The GitHub repository and the Python package on PyPI also went silent around the same time. Kokoro is supported by developer tools from Google, NVIDIA, and Intel, including software for voice agents and on-device speech synthesis. AMD and Amazon Web Services have also published guides demonstrating its use in AI-agent workflows. Hertz and his team took control of the Kokoro account on Hugging Face by simply registering the domain used by the original owner and resetting the login password. Over the past weekend, the researchers registered the “hexgrad.com” domain listed on Kokoro’s public DONATE.md file and used it to perform a password reset on the publisher’s account. They then ran a controlled test in which they modified Kokoro’s model weights in 87 seconds using a gaming GPU, causing the model to produce poisoned output. Hertz says the team tested the modified Kokoro model locally using its normal inference pipeline, but never uploaded the modified weights to Hugging Face, as that would likely put at risk many production systems depending on the model. The researcher underlines that an update would still carry all the hallmarks of a legitimate release, as tests from another account showed that Hugging Face would not flag anything as suspicious. story|ver:0.5|variant:flash,speech|title.content_excerpt: Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. story|ver:7.5|title:how we raised databr.content_excerpt: Why adaptive concurrency limits work better than fixed request-rate limits for long-running operations. As part of the Compute Platform team at Databricks, we turn cloud infrastructure into clusters ready to run customer workloads. Our day-to-day work includes provisioning virtual machines and coordinating cluster creation across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Our goal is to keep these systems available while letting customers use as much capacity as we can safely provide. In this post, we'll explore why fixed request-rate limits can fall short for these long-running operations, how adaptive concurrency limits help, and what we learned applying them to cluster creation for Databricks classic compute. You don't need to know any of this to use Databricks, but if you're curious about what happens behind a Databricks Runtime cluster launch, join us for a look inside the kitchen. Historically, we protected the system with fixed request-rate limits, tested against different load patterns and failure scenarios. We scaled our services primarily by adding resources and adjusting per-customer limits. The combination of workloads and dependency failures made these limits increasingly difficult to test and tune. Conservative limits turned away customer requests despite spare capacity, yet kept accepting requests when our services or dependencies, such as cloud providers, slowed down. Engineers manually lowered limits to shed load during incidents and raised them again after recovery. Adaptive concurrency limits account for both unfinished work and changing system health. They let more work start when capacity is available and slow the pace when the system struggles, helping the service make progress with less manual tuning. A fixed API request-rate ceiling remains as a final safety guardrail against exceptionally high incoming traffic. The manager posts a fixed rule: accept at most ten new orders per minute, whatever is happening at the stove. Even with spare cooking capacity, the rule turns orders away.
